questions.question: What is the main job of the InnoDB redo log?
options: Store old row versions for rollback
Make committed changes durable cheaply via sequential write-ahead logging, replayed after a crash
questions.explanation: Redo records physical page changes sequentially at commit so dirty pages can be flushed lazily; crash recovery replays it. Old versions live in undo; the binlog serves replication.

questions.question: Under REPEATABLE READ, session A reads a row, then session B updates and commits it. What does A see if it reads the row again in the same transaction?
options: The original value, because A reuses the read view from its first consistent read
The new value, because B committed
An error, because the row changed
A blocks until B's transaction is purged
questions.explanation: REPEATABLE READ keeps one read view for the whole transaction; older versions are reconstructed from undo. READ COMMITTED would show the new value.

questions.question: Which problem does the doublewrite buffer solve?
options: Duplicate primary keys during bulk inserts
Replication lag between primary and replica
Torn pages caused by a crash partway through writing a 16 KB page
questions.explanation: Pages are written to the doublewrite area first, so a partially written page can be restored from an intact copy before redo is applied.

questions.question: With `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2`, what can be lost?
options: All uncommitted and committed data since startup
About the last second of committed transactions if the OS crashes or power fails; a mysqld-only crash loses nothing
About the last second of transactions even if only mysqld crashes, but nothing on power loss
questions.explanation: With 2 the redo is written to the OS cache at commit and fsynced roughly once per second, so it survives a mysqld crash but not an OS crash or power cut.
